title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure rather than a model error inside a newsroom. A synthetic video was made to look like a Mother Jones report, carrying the outlet's logo and fabricated comments attributed to its editor, and it asserted as fact that the Democratic National Committee paid $259 million to a CNN chief to promote gender transition among children. The false claim did not travel through any system Mother Jones controlled. It entered circulation on X through an account named Roman, and the outlet learned of it the way any reader would.

Detection fell to outsiders. A group called @antibot4navalny identified the operation, and Mother Jones had to complain to X before the post came down. X removed it for violating its trademark policy, which means the impersonated branding was the trigger, not the falsity of the payment claim. Catching this earlier would have required either the platform to treat a fabricated news report as its own category of violation or the outlet to monitor for its own name and logo being reused, and neither happened before the video reached 155,000 views on one post and 50,000 on a repost.

What is not established is the attribution and the purpose. The link to a network called Matryoshka, also known as Storm-1679, and the suggestion that the effort aims to help Republicans in the 2026 midterms come from reporting and from a third party's identification, not from a finding. The summary itself notes the current effort has not gained much reach.

reports.title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

summary:
A Russian disinformation network called Matryoshka, also known as Storm-1679, has spread a fake video that looked like a Mother Jones report. The video falsely said the Democratic National Committee paid $259 million to CNN chief Mark Thompson to promote gender transition among children. It used a fake Mother Jones logo and fake comments from editor Clara Jeffery. An X account named Roman posted it, and it got 155,000 views, while another account's repost got 50,000. Mother Jones complained to X, which removed the post for violating its trademark policy.

The network has also posted deepfakes of celebrities criticizing Democrats and fake reports about Democratic candidates, made to look like they came from major news outlets. A group called @antibot4navalny identified the operation. So far, the current effort has not gained much reach, but it may be aimed at helping Republicans in the 2026 midterms. It also notes that the Trump administration closed government units that tracked Russian disinformation, leaving the US less able to respond.
